extracted.intended_audience: writers, comedians, students of aesthetics/philosophy, and scholars of humour theory
extracted.subtask_description: A general philosophical account of what makes things laughable and how comic effects operate across forms (gestures, situations, words, characters), intended to guide understanding and the production/analysis of humor. Based on Henri Bergson's Essay 'Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of the Comic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may laugh at an animal or object only when you detect in it some human attitude or expression (e.g., laugh at a hat because of the human caprice that formed it). Use human behavior/attitude as the proper subject of comic treatment; avoid trying to make purely non-human phenomena laughable unless you humanize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABSENCE OF FEELING which usually accompanies laughter — the comic could not produce its disturbing effect unless it fell on the surface of a soul that is thoroughly calm and unruffled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter demands a momentary anesthesia of the heart: strong emotion (pity, deep sympathy) suppresses the comic. To produce or appreciate comedy, the audience must be able to detach emotionally and respond with intelligence rather than sentiment. Anti-pattern: trying to make an audience laugh at a scene while they are emotionally aroused; the comic effect will be blunted or disappear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social nature / need for echo
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter appears to stand in need of an echo; our laughter is always the laughter of a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects often depend on group recognition, shared customs, and mutual complicity; some jokes fail to translate because they reference a particular social group's ideas. For creators: consider audience context and the social 'freemasonry' of laughers. For evaluation: assess whether the effect presumes shared background or relies on solitary perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as a social corrective / social signification
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter must answer to certain requirements of life in common. ... Laughter, then, does not belong to the province of esthetics alone, since unconsciously ... it pursues a utilitarian aim of general improvement. ... Laughter must be something of this kind, a sort of SOCIAL GESTURE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter as a mechanism that curbs inelasticity and eccentricity in social behaviour — it 'restrains eccentricity' and 'softens down' mechanical inelasticities. When assessing comedy, consider its social function (does it correct, expose, or reinforce norms?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from mechanical inelasticity / automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY, just where one would expect to find the wide-awake adaptability and the living pliableness of a human being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects are produced when human behaviour resembles a machine: rigidity, momentum, repetition, or lack of adaptive response. Examples: runner who stumbles (momentum), victim of prank (habit continues despite changed circumstances). Evaluate degree of 'mechanical' quality to measure comic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary action / accidental comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the sudden change of attitude that raises a laugh, but rather the involuntary element in this change... The comic is therefore accidental: it remains, so to speak, in superficial contact with the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidental, involuntary slips or failures often produce immediate comic responses. Distinguish deliberate clowning (which can be comic for other reasons) from genuinely involuntary missteps; the latter often provoke stronger laughter because they reveal inelasticity unexpectedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internalisation: when automatism is supplied from within
rubrics_metrics.description: When mechanical rigidity no longer requires ... a stumbling-block ... but extracts by natural processes, from its own store, an inexhaustible series of opportunities for externally revealing its presence ... the comic will take up its abode in the person himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character whose internal dispositions (habit, absentmindedness, fixed idea) systematically produce comic outcomes is funnier because the cause is internal and persistent. For character comedy, craft recurring internal rigidities rather than relying solely on external gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of natural cause: the more natural the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects are intensified when their causes are seen as genuine, inevitable, or organically arising from the character or situation (e.g., Don Quixote falling because of his romantic obsession). In comedy writing, deepen the perceived naturalness/necessity of the cause to heighten laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness as a key comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness ... is not perhaps the actual fountain-head of the comic, but surely it is contiguous to a certain stream of facts and fancies which flows straight from the fountain-head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absentminded characters (thinking of the past or of imaginary surroundings rather than the present) produce coherent, cumulative comic mishaps. Use systematic, organized distraction around a central idea to create escalating comic situations. Example: the over-romantic man walking like a somnambulist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice as external rigidity (comic vs tragic vices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice capable of making us comic is ... that which is brought from without, like a ready-made frame into which we are to step. It lends us its own rigidity instead of borrowing from us our flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic vices are those that appear as pre-formed, schematic defects (e.g., miserliness in Harpagon) rather than passions fully incarnated; they remain identifiable as types. For characterization, exaggerate a vice as a template or puppet that the character wears rather than as a tragic inner consuming passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic character is unconscious of self
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic character is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself. The comic person is unconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who do not perceive how they appear to others (lack of self-awareness) are more comic. When judging comic characters, consider how little they adapt or disguise their flaw when it's pointed out — that unawareness fuels laughter and can be used deliberately in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable deformity is imitable by a normal person
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person, could successfully imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For physical comedy or caricature, choose traits that suggest a gesture or attitude an ordinary person could mimic; the possibility of imitation reveals the mechanical/learned nature of the deformity. Anti-pattern: deformities that are wholly outside normal human imitation often evoke pity or horror rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic expression = unique, permanent grimace (promises nothing more than it gives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic expression of the face ... is a unique and permanent grimace. One would say that the person's whole moral life has crystallised into this particular cast of features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic facial expressions are stereotyped and fixed rather than expressive of mobile inner life. In visual comedy or acting, favor stable, 'promiseless' expressions that suggest petrified automatism. Contrast with expressive beauty, which suggests mobility and potential change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature reveals latent tendency via exaggeration (exaggeration as means)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the caricaturist consists in detecting ... an imperceptible tendency, and in rendering it visible to all eyes by magnifying it. For exaggeration to be comic, it must not appear as an aim, but rather as a means ... to make manifest ... the distortions which he sees in embryo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective caricature detects an incipient tendency in nature and amplifies it along its natural vector. Avoid gratuitous or arbitrary exaggeration that doesn't feel like an organic extension of the subject's real inclination; the best exaggeration feels inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestures/movements laughable in proportion as they resemble a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess or design physical comedy by how clearly and subtly a body can be read as 'jointed' or puppet-like while still appearing alive. The more perfectly the images of person and machine fit, the stronger the comic effect. For actors/dancers, aim for simultaneous suggestion of life and mechanical regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition / predictability of gesture causes laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: If I notice [a repeated gesture] and it succeeds in diverting my attention, if I wait for it to occur and it occurs when I expect it, then involuntarily I laugh. Why? Because I now have before me a machine that works automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use predictable, repetitive movements in performance to signal automatism. But repetition must be perceived and expected by the audience; timing and rhythm matter. Overuse can dull the effect; the audience must first sense the mechanical regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes automatism and provokes laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: To imitate any one is to bring out the element of automatism he has allowed to creep into his person. And as this is the very essence of the ludicrous, it is no wonder that imitation gives rise to laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody and mimicry work because they isolate and reproduce the mechanical elements of a subject's behaviour. In evaluating imitations, check whether the mimicry highlights mechanical uniformities rather than merely mocking mannerisms without revealing underlying automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody device: reassign gestures to mechanical occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: It will become even more [laughable] when it busies itself in deflecting them, though without altering their form, towards some mechanical occupation, such as sawing wood, striking on an anvil, or tugging away at an imaginary bell-rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodic interpretation often increases comedic effect by suggesting that a gesture is actually performing a banal mechanical task. Use such recontextualization to make elegant gestures appear absurdly utilitarian; it's a favored device of clowns and parodists.
